I spent a while building an agentic workflow engine called weft, making a set of small architectural decisions that all felt local at the time: where a package lives, which way an import points, whether the workflow is data or code, how the UI talks to the runtime. Later I read the platform-engineering write-ups in this same folder and had an uncomfortable recognition. The rules I'd fought my way to for turning a one-off tool into a reusable engine were the same rules those docs give for turning internal tooling into a platform. Different vocabulary, same boundary.

This piece draws that throughline: five decisions I made building weft, each a different angle on a single seam, and each already named in the [control-plane patterns write-up](/blog/platform-engineering) and the [PAVED build guide](/blog/building-a-platform) as the thing that makes a platform a platform.

## The second consumer is what makes it a platform

The origin story of weft was a good insight that almost wrecked the project. I decided the real product wasn't the software factory I was building; it was the engine underneath it, a general thing that could run any agentic workflow, of which "build software" was just use-case number one. I was proud of that. Then the very next thing I wanted to do was go build the clean, generic, domain-agnostic core immediately, before a second use-case existed anywhere except in my head.

That's the trap, and it's subtle: you design a general abstraction when you have exactly one example of the thing it's meant to generalize. Your single use-case quietly dictates the shape of every "generic" seam and you never catch it, because nothing argues back. You end up with an app wearing an engine's Halloween costume. Most of us already know the rule in some form; Sandi Metz put the sharpest version in ["The Wrong Abstraction"](https://sandimetz.com/blog/2016/1/20/the-wrong-abstraction) - duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction. It rhymes with Dijkstra's older point that abstraction exists to let you be more precise, not vaguer. An abstraction built against one example is just vagueness with good posture. The hard part isn't knowing this; it's believing it while you're excited, which is exactly when you meet it.

"Might need it someday" is not the trigger. The trigger is a second consumer that's actually committed and imminent, one you can name and design against. Can you point at consumer number two, or are you generalizing against your own imagination?

A platform is the same bet, scaled up. The [platform-engineering write-up](/blog/platform-engineering) opens on the central team that "works at 20 engineers and collapses at 200," and the whole federation move is a response to the second, third, and tenth consumer of a capability. One team asking for a Postgres database gets you a script. A platform is what you get when the second team asks and you refuse to fork the script for them. Extracting the engine and extracting the platform are the same restraint performed at the moment a second consumer forces your hand - not before, when the seam is imagination, and not after, when it's surgery.

## Dependency direction is the federation boundary

When it came time to turn weft's abstract layering into real directories and package names, it felt like a pile of taste decisions. What do I call the engine, where does the domain live, do I keep a shared-contracts package. None of it was taste. Dependency direction decided every one of those questions, and this is Uncle Bob's territory - the Dependency Inversion Principle, Clean Architecture, the Acyclic Dependencies Principle. A lot of engineers break out in hives at "Clean Architecture" and some of that allergy is earned, but "dependency direction is the architecture" is the gold nugget buried in the sermon.

Order the packages by how depended-upon they are. The most depended-on package sits at the bottom and has to be the leanest, because everything above inherits its dependencies; a fat package at the bottom poisons the whole tree. Do that honestly and the layout imposes itself: base conventions at the bottom, pure and tiny; the reusable engine in the middle, depending only on the base; the domain on top, depending on the engine; the things the system produces off to the side, depending on nothing internal.

The sharpest sub-rule, and the one I almost got wrong: the type that describes a package's output belongs in that package, not in a shared bucket. We nearly parked a report type in a shared-contracts package purely out of habit - that's where types go, right? But the report is produced by the low-level, deliberately-lean tool, and the shared bucket sat above that tool in the layering. Filing the type up in the bucket would have forced the lean tool to depend on a higher layer, dragging heavier dependencies down into the leanest thing in the tree. One lazy import and the base of the pyramid gets fat. So the type moves home to the package that produces it. Ownership follows production: you keep what you make.

That last sentence is the federation boundary word-for-word. The platform-engineering doc's whole argument is realigning authority with responsibility so "the team that writes a domain's logic is the team accountable for it," and its warning against a "communal sock drawer" of shared schemas is the same warning I hit with the report type. The engine never imports the domain. A platform's core never depends on any one consumer, and the security team owns the security contract rather than parking it in a central bucket the platform team then has to maintain. Same arrow.

And I made the arrow executable, which is the part that survives contact with a tired engineer at 2am: a policy check that fails the build when a low layer imports a high one. The layout stops being a diagram taped to the wall and becomes an invariant the gate won't let me violate. That's the same instinct the platform docs describe as moving policy to the control plane instead of trusting each pipeline to behave - the guardrail lives once, at the boundary every request must cross, and can't be dodged. Principles get rationalized away on a Friday. Gates don't negotiate.

## The engine is the drivetrain; the consumer drives

A reusable core has to run an application's logic without depending on the application. Those two requirements sound like they cancel - run the app's code, but don't import the app - and resolving that apparent contradiction is the entire game of reusability. The knot is that "depends on" is doing two jobs and people blur them: who imports whom, and who calls whom. Separate them and it falls apart. The dependency arrow points one way, the app imports the core. Control flows both ways, but only through objects the app hands to the core. The core exposes interfaces and primitives; the app implements them and does the driving; the core invokes the app's logic solely through the injected instances, never through an import. Martin Fowler's writing on Inversion of Control gave me the vocabulary to keep "imports" and "calls" from collapsing, and it bottoms out in the old Hollywood Principle: don't call us, we'll call you.

The picture I kept in my head was a car engine. It exposes a driveshaft, a throttle input, some mounting points, a fuel line. It turns the driveshaft when the throttle tells it to. It does not know what car it's bolted into, does not know where that car is going, and is emphatically not steering. The same engine drops into a sedan or a truck because it depends on none of them. Your reusable core is the engine; each application is a different car. An engine that knew the route would only fit one car, and then you'd have built a car.

This is control inversion, and it's exactly what a platform does to the org chart. The platform provides capability; the consumer drives. The [PAVED guide](/blog/building-a-platform) is emphatic that the platform team "stops writing domain logic and starts providing the substrate on which domain teams write their own" - the mall builds the power and plumbing and foot traffic, each vertical stocks its own storefront. The mall operator turning the driveshaft; the tenant picking the destination. A platform that knew every consumer's route would fit exactly one consumer, which is the re-centralized queue the whole model exists to escape.

There's a corollary that's the most useful sentence I got out of the whole exercise: the surface the app provides is the core's true public API. Not the core's exported functions - the list of everything the application hands the core: its workflows, its step implementations, its configuration, its entrypoint. That's the API that matters, and a single consumer cannot validate it, because one application will quietly shape the "generic" surface to its own contours and neither of you will notice. The second car is what proves the engine was ever an engine - which loops back to the second consumer. The reason you keep the surface explicitly unstable until a genuinely different consumer drives the same interfaces is the reason you don't extract until consumer two arrives.

## Declarative surface, imperative core: the platform contract, made mechanical

"Should the workflow be declarative or imperative" is a false binary that dissolves the moment you notice something always has to walk the data. A declarative recipe gets compiled into imperative execution anyway; there is always something that walks the structure and does the work. So declarative-versus-imperative was only ever a question about the authoring surface, never about how execution happens, which means you can have both.

Weft ended up with three pieces. One imperative interpreter, written once, owned by the engine - an event-iterator that walks a recipe and yields typed events, suspending and resuming as it goes, and nothing else is allowed to drive execution. A declarative recipe that is pure data: an ordered set of nodes, each a named step executor plus a transition, printable and diffable and validatable, its current position just a serializable pointer. And imperative step executors that are plain code. The structure is data, the driver is code, the work is code, and there is deliberately no workflow DSL anywhere. The one rule that keeps it from rotting into a framework: transitions are pure functions, not data conditions. A branch is `transition(state, result) -> next_node_id`, a small pure callable. The instant you let conditions become data like `{"if": {"field": "x", "op": "gt"}}` you're building the exact DSL you were avoiding, one operator at a time.

That split is the platform contract with the labels filed off. The [platform-engineering doc](/blog/platform-engineering) names the three properties that make a contract strong enough to federate on: a declarative request (state the outcome, `storageGB: 20`, never the procedure), schema validation at the boundary, and opaque fulfillment (the producer can swap Terraform for Pulumi and no consumer notices). My declarative recipe is the request the consumer authors; my imperative interpreter and executors are the opaque fulfillment nobody upstream should see. Kubernetes draws the exact same line and hands it to you for free: a CustomResourceDefinition registers the typed, validated contract, a controller supplies the behavior, and `spec` versus `status` splits the declared intent from the messy reported reality behind separate endpoints. Consumers declare intent; the imperative fulfillment stays hidden. I built by hand the seam that Kubernetes ships as its core abstraction, and I only recognized it as the same seam after reading the k8s patterns back.

One honest caveat, because the payoff sounds too clean. Because a run's position is a node id plus typed state, both serializable, resume across a restart comes back at node granularity with no durable-execution framework. That's a simpler path to the same place Temporal gets you, not proof Temporal is wrong, and I don't yet have evidence on which wins under real load. A bet I liked enough to build, not a scoreboard I've won.

## The interface is a queue, which is to say it's swappable

During the design of weft the AI I was sparring with recommended a synchronous engine, one the interface pumps in a loop, and argued it well. I didn't buy it, because there are two concurrencies hiding under that one word and they're unrelated: the engine parallelizing its own work, and the human interacting while the engine works. You can defer the first for a long time. You cannot defer the second if the product is interactive, because it's the entire difference between a shell and a batch job.

So the shape is two tasks over a typed queue pair: an interface task that owns human input and output, an engine task that runs the work, talking over an engine-to-interface event stream and an interface-to-engine command channel. The human types while the engine runs because neither blocks the other, and it's less code than the loop it replaced. The payoff I didn't fully see until later is that the queue pair isn't plumbing between the interface and the engine - it is the seam. Swap the REPL task for a terminal-UI task or a web/API task and the engine never finds out which one it's talking to, because all it ever sees is the queues. An interface you can't name is an interface you can't swap; a queue is nameable. Suspension, approval, and cooperative interrupt all fall out as await-on-a-queue rather than special machinery, and the one load-bearing rule - Rob Pike's "don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating" - is what keeps the two tasks from reinventing the races the split existed to kill.

This is the same decoupling the platform docs call "one contract-bearing plane" and "the interface is a facade over the contract, never a second path around it." The queue routes everything through one nameable seam so either side can be replaced without the other noticing - a REPL today, a web API tomorrow, the way a platform lets a consumer hit the same contract through `kubectl`, a Backstage form, or a Terraform module and get the identical request. The queue also fixes a mistake platforms make constantly: don't make your event store the streaming channel. The live stream the engine yields is the primary channel; the store is something the engine also writes to, for audit and resume. Weld streaming to the database and a library you wanted to call from a plain session suddenly needs a server to show its own progress bar. The database is a witness, not a messenger.

## One boundary, five angles

None of these five was a tip. Extract at the second consumer, point the dependency arrow one way, invert control so the consumer drives, split the declarative surface from the imperative core, and route the seam through a queue - they are one boundary seen from five sides. The boundary between the general thing and the specific thing that uses it. Draw it once, honestly, and the engine's package layout, its API, its execution model, and its I/O all fall out of the same line. Refuse to draw it and you get an app in an engine costume, which is the tooling version of a platform team that's responsible for everything and has authority over nothing.


The cheapest place to draw the boundary is a diagram, a name, and a lint rule, before either the engine or the platform exists. Everything after that moment is you paying retail: extracting a framework from an app, or dismantling a central team back into a federation, one furious consumer at a time. So the concrete move, whether you're writing a runtime or standing up a platform, is to make the arrow executable the day you name it. Write the build gate that fails when the low layer imports the high one. That single check is what makes the boundary real, and it costs a diagram now or a death march later.
